title: SeIM: In-Memory Acceleration for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
problem: ANNS workloads bottleneck on memory bandwidth (extensive random access) and sorting (cross-memory-unit data dependencies), limiting throughput in CPU/GPU/ASIC-based systems and making them inefficient for RAG-based LLM inference.
motivation: RAG is increasingly critical for LLM applications requiring up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge; ANNS is a primary latency/power bottleneck in RAG pipelines.
method: The system places approximate nearest neighbor search operations at different levels of the memory hierarchy based on their data-access patterns. Vector loading and distance computation—which read large amounts of data—run directly at the memory bank level (the hardware storage where data is kept), while sorting runs at the memory controller level (the hardware that manages data access) with selective filtering to block unnecessary data transfers. Since computation happens where data already is, there's no need for costly back-and-forth movement to the CPU or GPU. The architecture requires only minimal modifications to existing DRAM.
key_novelty: Approximate nearest neighbor search operations are distributed across the memory hierarchy—placing computation at the bank and controller levels where data naturally resides—using a unified execution model to eliminate redundant data transfers and reuse existing hardware.
contributions: 268–22× throughput improvement over CPU/GPU/ASIC ANNS systems
3081–2× power efficiency gain; only lightweight DRAM modifications required
Adaptive transmission filtering to reduce sorting overhead
limitations: Assumes standard DRAM-based memory hierarchies; scalability to multi-socket systems and interaction with prefetchers not discussed; comparison limited to existing ANNS accelerators.
primary_theme: hierarchical in-memory acceleration for ANNS via bank/controller-level partitioning
